analysis.one_liner: Bans medical debt from appearing on credit reports or being used in lending decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill would have kept medical debt off credit reports and out of lending decisions, but it died in the Senate Banking Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal credit law so that medical debt—bills people owe for doctors, hospitals, and medicine—could never appear on a person's credit report, even if sent to a collection agency. It would also require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules within one year barring lenders from looking at medical debt when deciding whether to approve a loan, credit card, or mortgage. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 100 million Americans who carry some medical debt, including people who paid their bills but still have collections on their reports. Medical bills are a leading driver of bad credit, which raises the cost of mortgages, car loans, credit cards, rentals, and even some job screening. Removing medical debt from credit reports would raise credit scores for millions and cut borrowing costs, and lenders could no longer deny credit based on unpaid hospital bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans with medical debt on their credit reports

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that no medical debt—including debt sent to a collection agency—can appear on a consumer's credit report.
It directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to change its rules within one year so creditors cannot obtain or use medical debt information when deciding whether to lend.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and debt collectors would lose the leverage of reporting medical debt, and lenders would lose a data point they use in underwriting. Hospitals and medical providers could still bill and sue for unpaid care, but might see slightly lower repayment rates if collections carry less threat.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders

drawbacks.text: Some lenders argue credit scores help predict repayment; removing medical debt changes the risk information they can use, which lenders and credit bureaus could claim leads to less tailored underwriting or higher prices for some borrowers.
The bill would not cancel or forgive any medical debt itself—people would still owe the money, and medical providers and collectors could still pursue payment directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending credit damage from illness—is real and the cost to lenders appears minimal, since medical debt is a poor predictor of loan repayment. The bill stalled without committee action in the 118th Congress, so no weighing of tradeoffs ever occurred on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill once and referred it to the Banking Committee, which never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended, so it expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 19, 2023, and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill died automatically when the Congress ended, as bills do not carry over.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, lenders, and debt collectors who benefit from keeping medical debt on credit reports; the roughly 100 million Americans with medical debt did not get the relief the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, lenders, and debt collectors

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip medical debt from credit reports and bar lenders from using it.

for.name: Sens. Robert Menendez, John Fetterman, and Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Senate support it attracted.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its referral—no markup, hearing vote, or report—keeping it from ever reaching the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but no vote was ever taken so the chamber's actual split was never tested.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and medical debt buyers
industries.note: They could still collect medical bills directly, but could no longer use credit reporting as leverage, which is a key tool for pressuring people to pay. The threat of a damaged credit score is often what makes patients settle.

Credit bureaus would lose data they currently include in reports, and lenders could no longer use medical debt in underwriting. Critics of the change argue medical debt is a weak predictor of repayment anyway, limiting the loss.
Losing credit-report leverage may reduce repayment rates on unpaid medical bills, shifting some cost onto providers, though the bill would not erase the debts themselves.
